title: East Asia Researcher
content: The Committee to Protect Journalists is seeking an East Asia Researcher, who will work in collaboration with the Asia-Pacific Regional Director and Asia-Pacific Program Coordinator, and is responsible for monitoring, researching, documenting, and responding to attacks on the press and other issues impacting press freedom in the region – primarily in China and Hong Kong, as well as Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and Mongolia. The researcher also assists the Asia-Pacific Program with advocacy efforts.

title: ‘Investigative Journalism Goes Beyond Numbers:’ Reporting on Health and the Environment in Côte d’Ivoire
content:
Marthe Akissi Kra is a familiar voice on Côte d’Ivoire’s public broadcaster Radiodiffusion Télévision Ivoirienne (RTI), where she reports on environmental conservation, sustainable development, health, and community affairs in the West African country.

She spends much of her time in the field reporting on the effects of climate change in Côte d’Ivoire and for Ivorians, such as the pressures facing protected areas — gold mining, population growth, the loss of its rainforests, poaching — and the environmental and health implications for local communities on the frontlines.

Kra has won several regional and international awards for her work, including the Media for Science and Development Award’s Super Prize for science journalism (Cote d’Ivoire), the second Norbert Zongo African Investigative Journalism Prize (PAJI-NZ) in the radio category, and the 2022 Prix Eco-Reportages du club de la presse Drôme-Ardèche (France). She was also recently selected Country Coordinator for the Network of Science Journalists for Francophone Africa (RSAF-Côte d’Ivoire).

title: GIJN Masterclass Round-Up: Artificial Intelligence
content:
GIJN’s Global Academy is your gateway to investigative journalism training. Through masterclass videos, training programs (in person or online), webinars or mentorship programs, the Academy helps journalists at every stage strengthen their investigative skills, connect with peers, and continue learning. In this post, we’ve gathered some of our recent expert masterclass videos that tackle different aspects of investigating AI as well as responsibly and ethically using it in your reporting.

In this masterclass video, Gabriel Geiger, investigative journalist at Lighthouse Reports, shares practical tips for reporting on how governments use algorithms and AI systems in public services such as policing, welfare, and healthcare.

Geiger explains how reporters can start investigating these systems by identifying government processes that may rely on automation, such as benefits decisions or risk assessments. Key reporting strategies include requesting documents and data about the systems, filing targeted freedom-of-information requests, and building sources inside institutions that interact with the technology.

title: Investigating Technology and AI in Conflict
content:
Reporting on modern warfare no longer relies solely on focusing on what is happening on the front line. Journalists must also show how the technologies and AI systems increasingly shaping conflict are conceived, financed and coded in conference rooms, data centres and technology offices far from the battlefield.

In this emerging military-technological complex, a new phase of the military-industrial complex, cloud platforms, AI models, and commercial infrastructure have become integral to the conduct of war. Yet this weaponization of technology makes accountability harder to trace than ever.

War reporters need more than flak jackets and nerves of steel. They must also dig into procurement records, trade databases, export licenses, corporate filings, and the digital breadcrumbs left behind by the military-tech ecosystem to understand complicity and responsibility in conflict.

In this workshop, based on an upcoming GIJN reporting guide, Dr. Iain Overton will introduce a practical framework for investigating the technological systems behind modern warfare, from surveillance infrastructure and automated decision-making to the financial flows that make them possible.

title: 10 Practical Tips for Verifying Scientific Claims
content:
A paper published in a scientific journal can seem like a promising lead for a news story or the beginning of an investigation. Yet peer review does not involve repeating every experiment or verifying every piece of data. Research may contain methodological flaws or unintentional errors; sometimes, the data have been manipulated or fabricated.

In 2025, journalist Frederik Joelving and computer scientists Cyril Labbé and Guillaume Cabanac published the findings of a six-month investigation into so-called scientific paper mills. These paper mills are businesses that produce and sell fraudulent scientific papers, often using fabricated or manipulated data.

Among the cases they examined was one in which a paper was first questioned by cancer researchers Soren Zielske and Danny Welch. The two scientists had tried to build on its findings but could not reproduce the results. Looking more closely, they found identical data in graphs that were supposed to represent different experiments. In 2020, Zielske posted his concerns on PubPeer and contacted the journal’s editor. The paper was later retracted for “falsified materials and/or data.”

title: Spain’s Solar Eclipses, Russia-Ukraine Drone Warfare, ICE Detention Camp Overcrowding, and Tracking the Spread of Fake News
content: As large swaths of Europe and parts of North America and Africa prepared for a solar eclipse this week, news outlets sought to capture the rare astronomical event that many people may never see again in their lifetime. El Orden Mundial’s visual story explored why Spain is one of the exceptions, with the country set to experience two more eclipses within two years. Our roundup of the Top 10 in Data journalism, looking at stories from July 23 to August 11, also includes a Reuters graphical illustration showing how drones are transforming fighting on the frontlines in Ukraine, an ARIJ investigation examining civilian-to-combatant casualty ratios in the Middle East under different US presidents, and a Straits Times analysis modeling how early debunking can stop the spread of misinformation.

title: Investigating Inside Conflict Zones and Areas Controlled by Armed Groups: Lessons from South Asia and the Middle East
content:
In October 2021, journalist Shahid Zehri was driving home to Karachi through the town of Hub, in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, when a bomb planted under his car seat detonated. He died of his injuries hours later.

The Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), a separatist rebel group regarded as a terrorist organization by the Pakistani government and several other countries, including the United States, claimed responsibility, accusing Zehri of spying for Pakistan’s security forces, without offering evidence. “It is intolerable that separatist rebels are able, with impunity, to claim the right to kill journalists in a completely arbitrary manner,” Reporters Without Borders (RSF) spokesperson Pauline Adès-Mével said in a statement in response to the killing.

title: Silencing Journalists Online: How Copyright Is Being Weaponized Against Investigative Journalists
content:
A new form of censorship is emerging globally to silence the work of journalists and activists. On digital platforms like Facebook or Google, journalists’ social media accounts and their stories are being targeted with fake complaints aimed at silencing their work online.

The perpetrators are often shady firms hired by powerful interests who offer to remove content their clients don’t like online by playing with digital platforms rules.

Reputation cleaning firms or individuals make up false claims of copyright infringement and pressure the digital platforms to take down targeted contents. Do they succeed? Often, they do.  And Big Tech companies sometimes even refuse to disclose information on who makes these complaints.

The mechanics are straightforward and hard to fight: scammers duplicate the journalists’ social media accounts or content and file fake copyright infringement claims to digital platforms, accusing the journalists of impersonating them thus violating the platforms’ rules. This results in the journalists’ accounts or posts being suspended or banned, with the victims sometimes not being aware of the reasons they’re kicked out.

title: Strategies To Seek Funding For Investigative Journalism
content:
We are in a challenging environment for investigative journalism. The need for investigative reporting exceeds reliable funding sources for it in many parts of the world. Nonetheless, investigative journalists are approaching the challenges with creativity and resilience, and have multiple paths to explore to seek funding. This session will provide a kind of decision tree or logic to help journalists determine what paths may be worth exploring to find story and project funding in their region or topic. Our talk is aimed at individual journalists who have not done fundraising for their work and are seeking advice on where to get started. We’ll explore key considerations and pathways you can choose depending on your circumstances to explore funding options and pursue those that may fit for you and support the journalism you seek to produce.

This session will not provide suggestions or lists of specific funding sources.  Funding options vary greatly by country, region and even your own individual situations. However, a tip sheet will provide links to global organizations that can help you research grant options, examples of journalism networks and networked funders and some other tips.
